## **Statement of the Problem** {#statement-of-the-problem}

The project tackles content-based fashion recommendations by combining natural language understanding with visual similarity matching. The system classifies fashion items according to their usage context using the labels available in the Fashion Product Images dataset from Kaggle (e.g., Casual, Formal, Sports, Ethnic, Party, and others found in `styles.csv`). Beyond this classification, it implements semantic search and ranking capabilities to retrieve visually and contextually relevant outfits. By using text queries to navigate image embeddings, the system effectively bridges the gap between natural language descriptions and visual data.

The machine learning architecture integrates three core approaches that operate collaboratively. First, supervised classification is used to predict usage categories based on visual features extracted from the images. Second, cosine similarity–based retrieval ranks fashion items by measuring their distances within a shared embedding space, enabling more accurate item matching. Third, a multimodal learning aligns textual and visual representations, allowing the system to interpret user queries such as “formal business attire” and match them to relevant clothing items based solely on visual attributes.

## **Significance of the Project** {#significance-of-the-project}

Developing an intelligent outfit recommendation system carries significant implications across social, industrial, and academic dimensions. From a social perspective, this technology democratizes access to fashion advice for individuals who may not have the resources to consult personal stylists or fashion experts. By providing instant and context-aware outfit suggestions, the system reduces the decision fatigue many people experience daily in selecting their outfits while building confidence in dressing appropriately for various social and professional contexts. This is especially valuable for individuals entering new environments, such as corporate workplaces, formal events, or cultural occasions, where appropriate attire significantly impacts first impressions and social comfort.

The fashion e-commerce industry, valued at approximately $1.2 trillion globally, increasingly relies on intelligent recommendation systems to enhance user experiences and drive sales (Accenture, 2022). Traditional collaborative filtering approaches struggle with cold-start problems for new users and new items (Bobadilla, et al., 2012). This content-based system addresses these challenges by analyzing the visual properties inherent in clothing items rather than relying solely on user interaction history. Retailers can integrate such systems to help customers discover products that match their immediate needs, whether they be preparing for a job interview, planning vacation outfits, or building a professional wardrobe. Aside from e-commerce, virtual wardrobe platforms and styling apps can leverage this technology to offer personalized suggestions, while inventory management systems can better understand which style-occasion associations resonate with consumers.

## **Objectives** {#objectives}

	The project primarily aims to develop a functional text-to-image retrieval system that accepts natural language queries describing desired outfits or occasions and returns contextually appropriate outfit recommendations ranked by relevance. This involves training a usage classifier capable of predicting occasion categories from visual features, implementing a semantic similarity ranking mechanism to order recommendations according to user intent, and creating an end-to-end pipeline that seamlessly integrates data preprocessing, model inference, and result presentation.

	Furthermore, the project also focuses on rigorous evaluation and practical deployment. The system’s classification performance will be assessed across all usage categories using standard metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores. The quality of the embedding space will be analyzed through visualization techniques and similarity metric computations to ensure that semantically related fashion items group together appropriately. A functional web interface consisting of a FastAPI backend and a React frontend will be developed to demonstrate a real-world application, enabling users to interact with the system through an intuitive search interface.

## **Dataset** {#dataset}

	The Fashion Product Images Dataset from Kaggle is used for this project. It contains a comprehensive collection of 44,424 fashion products, each accompanied by a product image and rich metadata describing various attributes. The metadata, stored in a CSV file named styles.csv, provides ten descriptive columns for each product. Each item has a unique identifier (`id`) that maps to its corresponding image file. Gender categorization (`gender`) segments products into Men, Women, Boys, Girls, and Unisex categories. The hierarchical categorization system includes master categories (`masterCategory`), such as Apparel, Footwear, Accessories, Personal Care, and Free Items, which are further subdivided into subcategories (`subCategory`), such as Topwear, Bottomwear, Watches, and Eyewear, encompassing over 45 distinct categories. The most granular level, article type (`articleType`), specifies the exact item types, such as Shirts, Jeans, Watches, or Sunglasses, with over 140 distinct types represented in the dataset.

	Additional metadata includes the primary color (`baseColour`) with 47 unique colors, seasonal appropriateness (`season`) categorized as Fall, Summer, Winter, or Spring, and the product year (`year`) ranging from 2011 to 2017\. The `usage` column serves as the primary target variable for this project, classifying items into occasion-based categories, including Casual, Formal, Sports, Ethnic, Party, Smart, Casual, Travel, and Home. Finally, each product has a human-readable description (`productDisplayName`) that combines brand, target demographic, key features, and item type into a descriptive string.

	However, the dataset presents several quality considerations that must be addressed during preprocessing. Approximately five products lack corresponding image files, requiring validation checks to filter our incomplete entries. A significant class imbalance exists, where the “Casual” category dominates the dataset, comprising around 85% of all labeled items. This imbalance poses challenges for training balanced classifiers, as minority categories like “Party” and “Smart Casual” contain fewer than ten samples each. Some rows also contain missing values in non-critical columns, but these can be handled through imputation or by designating them as “Unknown” appropriately.

	Despite these downsides, the dataset is ideal for this project because its diverse product categories span complete outfits from tops and bottoms to accessories and footwear, enabling comprehensive outfit recommendations rather than focusing on a single clothing type. The rich metadata also supports multiple prediction tasks and allows sophisticated filtering and ranking strategies beyond simple visual similarity. Most importantly, the pre-labeled usage categories align perfectly with the project’s main objective of occasion-based recommendations.

## **Scope and Limitations** {#scope-and-limitations}

	The current implementation focuses exclusively on dataset-based recommendations. In other words, the system recommends items from the pre-indexed Fashion Product Images Dataset rather than analyzing user-uploaded personal wardrobe photos. This approach ensures the project remains feasible within the given timeframe.

### **Rationale** {#rationale}

* **Feasibility:** Manageable scope for a limited-time project  
* **Performance:** Pre-computed embeddings enable real-time response  
* **Use Case:** Acts as a fashion discovery tool, similar to a search engine for outfits

  ### **Scope** {#scope}

* Users can enter text, such as “casual summer outfit.”  
* The system can predict the usage based on the inputted text.  
* The system can retrieve matching products from the dataset based on the inputted text.  
* The system returns the top items with images and metadata based on the inputted text.

  ### **Limitations** {#limitations}

* The system does not allow users to upload images of personal clothing items.  
* The system does not have any user authentication involved, as it is designed to be a single-purpose website

## **Methods** {#methods}

### **Data Preprocessing** {#data-preprocessing}

	The data preprocessing pipeline begins with image validation to ensure data integrity. Each product identifier in the metadata is checked against the actual image files to filter out the lack of corresponding images for some products. This validation step prevents runtime errors during feature extraction, having robust error handling to properly skip corrupted or unreadable image files that might have been damaged during dataset distribution. The metadata found in the raw CSV data will also undergo a cleaning process to address several quality issues, including whitespaces and missing labels.

### **Feature Extraction** {#feature-extraction}

	The feature extraction process leverages a vision-language model for cross-modal understanding, such as CLIP ViT-B/32, to associate visual content with natural language descriptions through contrastive learning.

### **Usage Classification Model** {#usage-classification-model}

The project will use a classification algorithm, like Logistic Regression, for predicting usage categories from embeddings that prioritizes interpretability, speed, and effectiveness for this specific problem. 

### **Recommendation Pipeline** {#recommendation-pipeline}

	The recommendation system operates through a multi-stage ranking architecture that progressively narrows down candidates to deliver highly relevant results. This pipeline ensures that recommendations are both semantically meaningful and computationally efficient.

## **Ethical Considerations** {#ethical-considerations}

### **Bias in Fashion Data** {#bias-in-fashion-data}

* **Gender bias**: Dataset labeled by binary gender; not inclusive of non-binary individuals  
* **Cultural bias**: "Ethnic" category may not represent global fashion diversity  
* **Body type**: Models in the dataset may not reflect diverse body types  
* **Mitigation**: Acknowledge limitations; future work includes diverse data sources

### **Sustainability** {#sustainability}

* Encouraging outfit reuse and discovery (vs. fast fashion)  
* No promotion of overconsumption

## **Success Criteria** {#success-criteria}

	The project aims to implement a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) with the following features:

* Working text-to-recommendation pipeline  
* Classification accuracy \>75%  
* Basic web interface  
* Functional backend API

## **Conclusion** {#conclusion}

This project demonstrates a practical end-to-end machine learning system combining a vision-language model with a traditional machine learning classifier to solve a real-world problem in fashion e-commerce. The system's lightweight architecture and pre-computed embeddings make it deployable on standard hardware while maintaining strong performance.
